With an High Hand
with an HY HAND
n. phr. (of Israel's going out of Egypt, and of presumptuous sin)
Hebrew b'yād rāmāh — with a lifted or raised hand; rūm, to be high or exalted. The same phrase carries two opposite senses in the Law, according to whose hand is lifted.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

The AV keeps one idiom for two very different things, and the difference is everything. In Exodus and Numbers it describes the manner of the exodus: the children of Israel went out with an high hand — openly, in the sight of all the Egyptians, not slipping away by night as fugitives but marching out as a people redeemed, with the hand of their God lifted over them. It is a phrase of triumph and of public vindication, and it belongs to the LORD before it belongs to Israel; the psalmist praises Him who brought out Israel with a strong hand and a stretched out arm. In Numbers 15 the same words name the worst class of sin. Having provided offerings for the soul that sinneth through ignorance, the Law turns: the soul that doeth ought presumptuously — Hebrew, with an high hand — the same reproacheth the LORD; and that soul shall be cut off from among his people. There the lifted hand is the sinner's own, raised in defiance against God, and for it the sacrificial system makes no provision. The idiom thus marks the two directions a raised hand can take: God's hand lifted for His people in redemption, and a man's hand lifted against God in presumption.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): High-handed, overbearing; oppressive; violent. Hand, in Scripture, power, might, and the instrument of action. Exodus 14:8; Numbers 15:30.

expand to see more

High, elevated; lifted up; raised above a surface or the common level.

High-handed, overbearing; oppressive; violent; arbitrary.

Hand, in Scripture, power, might, the instrument by which a work is done.

Hebrew rūm, to be high, rise, be lifted up or exalted.

Presumptuously, with bold and insolent confidence. Numbers 15:30.

Key Scripture

Exo 14:8 — "And the LORD hardened the heart of Pharaoh king of Egypt, and he pursued after the children of Israel: and the children of Israel went out with an high hand."

Num 33:3 — "And they departed from Rameses in the first month, on the fifteenth day of the first month; on the morrow after the passover the children of Israel went out with an high hand in the sight of all the Egyptians."

Num 15:30 — "But the soul that doeth ought presumptuously, whether he be born in the land, or a stranger, the same reproacheth the LORD; and that soul shall be cut off from among his people."

Psa 136:12 — "With a strong hand, and with a stretched out arm: for his mercy endureth for ever."

Modern Corruption

The idiom is levelled into a single sense, so that the triumph of the exodus and the defiance of presumptuous sin are no longer distinguished; and presumptuous sin itself is softened into mere mistake.

expand to see more

Modern versions frequently render the two occurrences with unrelated English, which is defensible translation but costs the reader the deliberate echo. In Hebrew the same hand is raised in both places, and the Law intends the comparison: a people brought out under God's lifted hand are the last people who may lift their own against Him. Where the echo is lost, Numbers 15 reads as an isolated severity instead of the natural answer to Exodus 14, and the reader misses that presumption is not merely disobedience but the reversal of redemption's own gesture.

The more serious corruption is the quiet disappearance of the category. Numbers 15 distinguishes sin through ignorance, for which an offering is appointed, from sin with an high hand, for which none is, and the New Testament keeps the distinction in its own terms when it speaks of sinning wilfully after receiving the knowledge of the truth. A pastoral culture that treats all sin as weakness, inherited damage or poor choices has no way to name defiance, and therefore no way to call a man out of it. Scripture is tender toward the ignorant and the straying and hard toward the presumptuous, and the two must not be levelled. The principle to recover is that there is a sin which reproaches the LORD, and that the warning is mercy to the man still able to hear it.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew b'yād rāmāh, with a lifted hand — of Israel marching out in triumph, and of the sinner raising his hand against God.

expand to see more

Hebrew yād, hand; rāmāh, lifted or raised, from rūm.

In Exodus 14:8 and Numbers 33:3 the sense is open triumph, not stealth.

In Numbers 15:30 the AV renders the same idiom presumptuously.

The presumptuous soul reproacheth the LORD and is cut off from his people.

Compare the strong hand and stretched out arm of Psalm 136:12.

Usage

"the children of Israel went out with an high hand"

"the soul that doeth ought presumptuously"

"with a strong hand, and with a stretched out arm"
